payload.task_text:
I lead a research group and we're starting a deep dive into reasoning methods for large language models. There's a PDF in your workspace called Survey_Guidelines.pdf that outlines the structure we want, and a guide.md with some notes on how to organize the taxonomy and comparison criteria.

I need you to search for recent papers on chain-of-thought prompting, tree-of-thought reasoning, self-consistency decoding, step-by-step verification, and automatic chain-of-thought generation. There should be several relevant papers in the database. Download and read through them to understand the key contributions and methodologies.

Once you've reviewed the papers, write a comprehensive survey document called LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx. It should follow the structure in the guidelines: start with an abstract summarizing the survey, then an introduction to the field, a background section, a taxonomy of methods section broken into subsections for each reasoning approach, a comparative analysis section with a table comparing the methods, a section on open challenges, and a conclusion. Each method subsection should reference the corresponding paper and summarize the key ideas, methodology, and results. Make sure you cover at least five distinct reasoning methods. Use proper Word heading styles (Heading 1 / Heading 2) for the section and subsection titles so the document is well structured.

Also, create a database in our team's Notion workspace called "Reasoning Papers" to track these papers. The database should have these properties: Title (title type), Authors (rich_text), Year (number), Method (select), Key_Contribution (rich_text), and Cited_By (number). Add an entry for each relevant reasoning paper you found.

Finally, schedule five reading group sessions on the calendar for the week of March 16 through March 20, 2026. Each session should be one hour long and cover one paper. Title them "Reading Group: [short topic]" where the topic reflects the paper being discussed, like "Reading Group: Chain-of-Thought" or "Reading Group: Tree-of-Thought". Schedule them from 10:00 to 11:00 each day, Monday through Friday. Make the 10:00-11:00 wall-clock time unambiguous by providing the event times as UTC (for example "2026-03-16T10:00:00Z" or "2026-03-16T10:00:00"), or by supplying an ISO time with a timezone offset and passing the corresponding timeZone field (for example start time "2026-03-16T10:00:00+08:00" with timeZone "Asia/Shanghai").

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, the main agent must first read `Survey_Guidelines.pdf` and `guide.md` and freeze the document taxonomy and comparison fields. The guide does not identify papers, so for each literal method query `chain-of-thought prompting`, `tree of thoughts`, `self-consistency chain of thought`, `step-by-step verification`, and `automatic chain of thought`, the main agent must issue `search-arxiv(keyword=<method query>)` and `search_papers(query=<method query>,max_results=10)` as native-parallel discovery calls. Reconcile candidates by exact arXiv ID/title and freeze exactly one source-supported distinct `{method,paper_id,title}` assignment for each required method. Do not dispatch Wave 1 until all five literal assignments exist; report a discovery blocker rather than assigning an unnamed paper.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents in parallel:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): One explore sub-agent receives the literal chain-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, then returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): One explore sub-agent receives the literal tree-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): One explore sub-agent receives the literal self-consistency `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): One explore sub-agent receives the literal step-by-step verification `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): One explore sub-agent receives the literal automatic chain-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

After Wave 1, the main agent must reject a missing/mismatched ID, duplicate paper, or unsupported evidence field, freeze one canonical five-paper packet (method, paper_id, title, authors, year, key_contribution, results, cited_by), and derive the survey taxonomy and comparison rows from it.

2. Wave 2 — dispatch exactly 3 coder sub-agents in parallel:

   1. coder 0 (office-report-builder 0): The document coder sole-writes LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx in the workspace with the Word tools: document title/author metadata, then Title, Abstract, 1. Introduction, 2. Background, 3. Taxonomy of Methods (Heading-2 category subsections, Heading-3 per-method subsections), 4. Comparative Analysis containing a table with exactly the five required method columns populated from the frozen packet, and the remaining guideline-required sections; read the outline and full text back.
   2. coder 1 (external-workflow-operator 0): The Notion coder solely owns the Reasoning Papers database: search the workspace first and reuse an existing exact-title database, otherwise create it once under a suitable parent page with exactly the properties Title(title), Authors(rich_text), Year(number), Method(select), Key_Contribution(rich_text), Cited_By(number); add exactly five pages (one per frozen paper) with those properties, then retrieve the database and entries to verify.
   3. coder 2 (external-workflow-operator 1): The calendar coder schedules the five reading-group sessions for 2026-03-16 through 2026-03-20, each exactly 10:00-11:00 UTC (start/end dateTime with Z suffix and timeZone UTC), one per paper, with summary exactly 'Reading Group: <topic>' and a description naming the full paper title, first author, year and arXiv ID; search exact summaries first and create only missing events, then get_event every retained ID.

After Wave 2, the main agent reconciles the document outline/table, the five Notion entries and the five retained event IDs against the same canonical packet, then calls claim_done. Do not dispatch any further agent and do not add a verification wave.

Plan a multi-system research task. Workspace is strictly /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-scholarly-arxiv-survey-word-notion-gcal/workspace. User requests: inspect Survey_Guidelines.pdf and guide.md; research/download/read recent papers covering chain-of-thought prompting, tree-of-thought reasoning, self-consistency decoding, step-by-step verification, and automatic chain-of-thought generation; create comprehensive LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx with specified abstract/introduction/background/taxonomy subsections/comparative table/open challenges/conclusion and proper Heading 1/2; create Notion database “Reasoning Papers” with exact properties and entries for relevant papers; create five Google Calendar events March 16–20, 2026, 10:00–11:00 UTC, one paper/topic per day. Produce a concise execution plan, dependencies, likely canonical papers, and verification checklist. Read-only only; do not modify anything.
Plan survey workflow

Read and summarize the local requirement files at /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-scholarly-arxiv-survey-word-notion-gcal/workspace/Survey_Guidelines.pdf and /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-scholarly-arxiv-survey-word-notion-gcal/workspace/guide.md. Strictly remain inside that workspace. Return exact structural, length, taxonomy, comparison-table, formatting, and citation requirements relevant to building LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx. Do not modify files.
Inspect survey guidelines

Research and read five canonical papers for an LLM reasoning survey: (1) Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models, arXiv 2201.11903; (2) Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models, arXiv 2203.11171; (3) Zhang et al., Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models, arXiv 2210.03493 (verify ID); (4) Yao et al., Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models, arXiv 2305.10601; (5) Lightman et al., Let's Verify Step by Step, arXiv 2305.20050. Search, download if needed, and read full papers using scholarly/arXiv tools. Return a structured evidence pack per paper: exact title, full authors as given, year, arXiv ID, method label/category, contribution, methodology, models/datasets/benchmarks, exact headline numerical results with baselines, computational implications, task generality, limitations, and suggested short calendar topic. Include enough verified detail for a comprehensive survey and Notion entries. Read-only; do not create external records or local artifacts.
Research reasoning papers

Create and verify the Word document /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-scholarly-arxiv-survey-word-notion-gcal/workspace/LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx. Strict workspace boundary. Requirements from Survey_Guidelines.pdf and guide.md: title; Abstract 150–200 words; Heading 1 sections in order: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Taxonomy of Methods, Comparative Analysis, Open Challenges, Conclusion, References. Use Heading 2 for background subsections, taxonomy category headings and each of the five dedicated method subsections (or clear Heading 2 method subsections); taxonomy categories: Prompting-Based (CoT, Auto-CoT), Search-Based (Self-Consistency, Tree of Thoughts), Verification-Based (Process Supervision). Each method must state exact paper title/authors, key contribution/novelty, methodology, experimental benchmarks, main numerical results, computational cost, task generality, implementation complexity, and limitations. Comparative table must include columns Method Name, Paper Title, Accuracy Improvement, Computational Cost, Task Generality, plus Implementation Complexity. Add thoughtful synthesis, practical recommendations, open challenges, and consistent references with arXiv IDs. Proper actual Word Heading 1/Heading 2 styles required.
Use these verified facts:
CoT — “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models,” Jason Wei; Xuezhi Wang; Dale Schuurmans; Maarten Bosma; Fei Xia; Ed H. Chi; Quoc V. Le; Denny Zhou, 2022, arXiv 2201.11903. Manual few-shot rationales, one greedy path, no training. PaLM 540B GSM8K 56.9% vs standard prompting 17.9% (+39.0 pp). Benchmarks arithmetic GSM8K/SVAMP/ASDiv/AQuA/MAWPS; commonsense CommonsenseQA/StrategyQA; symbolic tasks. Scale-emergent, unfaithful possible, demonstration sensitivity.
Self-Consistency — “Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models,” Xuezhi Wang; Jason Wei; Dale Schuurmans; Quoc V. Le; Ed H. Chi; Sharan Narang; Aakanksha Chowdhery; Denny Zhou, 2022, arXiv 2203.11171. Sample diverse CoT paths, normalize answers, modal vote; no training. PaLM 540B GSM8K 74.4% vs ordinary CoT 56.9%; paper headline gains up to +17.9 GSM8K, +11.0 SVAMP, +12.2 AQuA, +6.4 StrategyQA, +3.9 ARC-Challenge; around 40 samples, diminishing returns. High Nx inference cost, weak for open-ended output, correlated majority errors.
Auto-CoT — “Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models,” Zhuosheng Zhang; Aston Zhang; Mu Li; Alex Smola, 2022, correct arXiv 2210.03629. Embed question pool, k-means clustering, choose representatives, zero-shot generate rationales with “Let’s think step by step,” then use as demonstrations. Ten datasets: SingleEq/AddSub/MultiArith/AQUA-RAT/GSM8K/SVAMP/CommonsenseQA/StrategyQA/Last Letter/Coin Flip. MultiArith 92.0% vs manual CoT 91.7%; matches/exceeds manual CoT on average in reported suite. Setup cost amortized, one test path, generated-rationale contamination risk.
Tree of Thoughts — “Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models,” Shunyu Yao; Dian Yu; Jeffrey Zhao; Izhak Shafran; Thomas L. Griffiths; Yuan Cao; Karthik Narasimhan, 2023, arXiv 2305.10601. Thought decomposition/generation/state evaluation/value or vote/search BFS or DFS with pruning/backtracking. GPT-4 Game of 24: ToT 74%, CoT 4%, best-of/self-consistency 9%, input-output ~7%; creative writing ~7.56 vs CoT ~6.19; mini-crossword ~60% word-level but ~4% full-grid. High multi-call cost/task engineering, evaluator error/combinatorial growth.
Process supervision — “Let’s Verify Step by Step,” Hunter Lightman; Vineet Kosaraju; Yura Burda; Harri Edwards; Bowen Baker; Teddy Lee; Jan Leike; John Schulman; Ilya Sutskever; Karl Cobbe, 2023, arXiv 2305.20050. PRM800K ~800k step-level human labels over MATH solutions; train PRM vs outcome reward model and rerank many candidates. Representative 500-problem MATH subset: PRM 78.2%, ORM 72.4% (+5.8 pp), majority 53.2%; headline scales to ~1,860 candidate solutions/problem. Expensive labels/training/inference, direct evidence math-focused, verifier gaming/local-vs-global concerns.
Important: percentages across papers are not directly comparable due to models/tasks/budgets. Build a polished, comprehensive research survey, then verify document outline, abstract word count, table existence/rows, and return path plus verification report. You may use office tools, python/docx, and Word inspection tools. Do not create Notion records or calendar events.
Build survey document

Create and verify a Notion database titled exactly “Reasoning Papers” in the connected team workspace. First search to avoid duplicating an existing database; if one already exists, verify/reuse it and add missing entries without duplicates. If none exists, choose an appropriate accessible team page as parent. Exact properties: Title (title), Authors (rich_text), Year (number), Method (select), Key_Contribution (rich_text), Cited_By (number). Create one entry for each of these five papers, with Cited_By set to a reasonable available numeric citation count if reliably obtainable from connected search, otherwise 0 (do not omit):
1) Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models — Authors: Jason Wei; Xuezhi Wang; Dale Schuurmans; Maarten Bosma; Fei Xia; Ed H. Chi; Quoc V. Le; Denny Zhou — Year 2022 — Method “Chain-of-Thought” — contribution: elicits explicit multi-step reasoning with few-shot rationale demonstrations and no parameter updates.
2) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models — Authors: Xuezhi Wang; Jason Wei; Dale Schuurmans; Quoc V. Le; Ed H. Chi; Sharan Narang; Aakanksha Chowdhery; Denny Zhou — Year 2022 — Method “Self-Consistency” — contribution: samples diverse CoT paths and selects the modal answer, improving reasoning accuracy without training.
3) Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models — Authors: Zhuosheng Zhang; Aston Zhang; Mu Li; Alex Smola — Year 2022 — Method “Automatic CoT” — contribution: automatically clusters questions and generates diverse zero-shot rationales for few-shot demonstrations.
4) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models — Authors: Shunyu Yao; Dian Yu; Jeffrey Zhao; Izhak Shafran; Thomas L. Griffiths; Yuan Cao; Karthik Narasimhan — Year 2023 — Method “Tree of Thoughts” — contribution: conducts explicit tree search over intermediate thoughts using generation, evaluation, pruning, and backtracking.
5) Let’s Verify Step by Step — Authors: Hunter Lightman; Vineet Kosaraju; Yura Burda; Harri Edwards; Bowen Baker; Teddy Lee; Jan Leike; John Schulman; Ilya Sutskever; Karl Cobbe — Year 2023 — Method “Process Supervision” — contribution: trains step-level process reward models with PRM800K and shows stronger selection than outcome supervision on MATH.
Acceptance: exact schema names/types, five unique entries, select options matching those method strings, no duplicate records. Return database ID/URL, entry IDs, Cited_By values used, and verification outcome. This is an authorized external write; do not modify local files or calendar.
Create Notion paper tracker

Create and verify exactly five Google Calendar events for the LLM reasoning reading group. First list events in the relevant date range to avoid duplicates; if matching events already exist, reuse and verify rather than duplicate. Each event is 10:00–11:00 UTC with timezone UTC, no recurrence, no attendees, blank location. Dates/titles/descriptions:
2026-03-16: “Reading Group: Chain-of-Thought” — discuss Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (arXiv:2201.11903).
2026-03-17: “Reading Group: Self-Consistency” — discuss Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (arXiv:2203.11171).
2026-03-18: “Reading Group: Automatic CoT” — discuss Zhang et al., Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models (arXiv:2210.03629).
2026-03-19: “Reading Group: Tree-of-Thought” — discuss Yao et al., Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models (arXiv:2305.10601).
2026-03-20: “Reading Group: Step-by-Step Verification” — discuss Lightman et al., Let’s Verify Step by Step (arXiv:2305.20050).
Use explicit ISO timestamps with Z or +00:00 and timeZone UTC. Return event IDs and exact start/end/timezone verification. Authorized external write; do not modify Notion or local files.
Schedule reading sessions
